provenance.rightsNote: Lectio Vernacular Edition (SDIT): a plain-modern-English rendering of Genesis, made from public-domain sources and the Hebrew text. This is Lectio's own edition, derived from public-domain sources — not a historical translation. DRAFT: in progress, and not yet read end to end by a human reviewer; the King James Version remains this work's default edition until it has been.
sourcesCited: Hebrew Bible, Leningrad Codex tradition — public domain

character: Plain modern English — the sense of the original, made to read with ease today.
overview: Genesis is spare where you expect grandeur. The Hebrew has a small vocabulary, repeats itself on purpose, and almost never explains — it tells you what happened and leaves the judgment to you. Four hundred years of English Bibles have added solemnity the Hebrew does not have. This edition takes it back out, keeps the refrains verbatim because they are the architecture, and lets the strangeness stand.
introduction:
Genesis holds two kinds of story. The first eleven chapters are about everyone — creation, a garden, a murder, a flood, a tower — told in a register closer to myth than to history, and they set the terms for everything after. Then the scale narrows to a single family: Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob, Leah, Rachel, Joseph. These people lie, cheat, favor one child over another, and are chosen anyway, and the book never once pauses to tell you what to think about it.

The Hebrew is the plainest prose in the Bible, and it is built on repetition: the same phrases return like structural beams, and the storytelling runs on 'and… and… and.' English translators have generally treated that as a defect to be fixed. It is not a defect. This edition keeps the refrains word for word, keeps more of the connective 'and' than modern prose taste wants, and marks the places where a pun in the Hebrew carries meaning that no English word can carry across.

divergences.older: “In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.” (KJV) — a complete sentence
divergences.lectio: “When God began to create the heavens and the earth —” a dependent clause resolved at verse 3
divergences.note: The Hebrew syntax more likely opens a dependent clause that runs until 'God said, Let there be light.' Creation begins not with a pronouncement but with a scene already dark and wet. Rashi read it this way in the eleventh century, and most modern scholarship agrees.

divergences.phrase: תֹהוּ וָבֹהוּ / רוּחַ אֱלֹהִים (tohu wabohu / ruach elohim)
divergences.older: “without form, and void” / “the Spirit of God moved” (KJV)
divergences.lectio: “a shapeless waste” / “the breath of God hovered”
divergences.note: The Hebrew is a rhyming pair meaning something like unformed-and-empty; 'without form, and void' is accurate and bloodless. Ruach means breath, wind, and spirit at once, and the verb is used elsewhere of an eagle fluttering over its young — a brooding bird, not a ghost.
Kept exactly, not out of deference to the King James Version but because it is the plain and exact rendering of three Hebrew words. Knowing what not to touch is most of this work.

divergences.lectio: rendered plainly, with the wordplay noted
divergences.note: In Hebrew the play is total: God forms the human (adam) out of the humus (adamah). The man is named for the dirt he comes from, and the whole sentence of 3:19 — 'to dust you will return' — is already folded into his name.

divergences.older: “an help meet for him” (KJV), later flattened to “a helper”
divergences.note: Ezer is used most often in the Hebrew Bible of God himself and carries no subordination; kenegdo means corresponding-to-him, his counterpart. 'Helper' imports a hierarchy the Hebrew does not have.

Everywhere else in the Hebrew Bible this word means the side of a thing — the side of the ark, of the altar, of a building. The woman is built from the man's side, not from a spare part. 'Rib' entered through the Greek translation and stuck for two thousand years.
The last word of chapter 2 is 'naked' and the first word about the serpent is 'cunning' — in Hebrew they are nearly the same word. No English pair carries it. It is the hinge the story turns on.

divergences.older: “the LORD” in small capitals (KJV and every English Bible since Tyndale)
divergences.note: The four-letter divine name is a name, not a title, and its pronunciation was deliberately given up. The small-capital substitution is honest — it marks that a substitution is happening — without inventing a pronunciation the tradition abandoned on purpose.

The Hebrew verb is the one used of an animal lying in wait. Sin here is not a stain but a predator at the threshold — and the sentence that follows says Cain can master it, which is why the image matters.

The Hebrew word is left untranslated because nobody knows what it means. 'Giants' is the Greek translators' guess, repeated for two thousand years; the honest thing is to keep the name and let the strangeness stand.

'Repent' now suggests turning from sin, which is not what the Hebrew says about God. The word is regret and grief — and the line that follows, 'it grieved him to the heart,' is the plainest statement of divine pain in the book.

divergences.older: “And God remembered Noah” (KJV) — kept, and easily misread
divergences.lectio: “And God remembered Noah” — kept, with the sense noted
divergences.note: The Hebrew verb does not mean God had forgotten. Remembering here is acting on a commitment — the hinge of the whole flood narrative, and the exact centre of its structure. The English word is right; the modern reading of it is not.

divergences.older: “Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be” (KJV)
divergences.lectio: “Cursed be Canaan. The lowest of slaves he will be to his brothers.”
divergences.note: The Hebrew says slave, not servant, and this edition does not soften it. The passage was used for centuries to justify the enslavement of Africans — a reading with no basis in the text, which curses Canaan, not Ham, and names a people in the land, not a race. Rendering it plainly is the only way to let a reader see what it does and does not say.

segments.text: When God began to create the heavens and the earth — the earth was a shapeless waste, darkness lay over the face of the deep, and the breath of God hovered over the waters — God said, “Let there be light.” And there was light. God saw that the light was good, and God separated the light from the darkness. God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And there was evening, and there was morning: the first day.

God said, “Let there be a vault in the middle of the waters, to separate water from water.” So God made the vault, and it separated the water beneath it from the water above it. And so it was. God called the vault Sky. And there was evening, and there was morning: the second day.

God said, “Let the waters under the sky be gathered into one place, so that dry land can appear.” And so it was. God called the dry land Earth, and the gathered waters he called Seas. And God saw that it was good. God said, “Let the earth put out growth: plants that seed themselves, and every kind of fruit tree bearing fruit with its seed inside it.” And so it was. The earth put out growth — every kind of seed-bearing plant, every kind of tree bearing fruit with its seed inside it. And God saw that it was good. And there was evening, and there was morning: the third day.

God said, “Let there be lights in the vault of the sky to separate day from night. Let them mark the seasons, the days, and the years, and let them shine in the vault of the sky to light the earth.” And so it was. God made the two great lights — the greater light to govern the day, the lesser light to govern the night — and the stars. God set them in the vault of the sky to light the earth, to govern day and night, and to separate light from darkness. And God saw that it was good. And there was evening, and there was morning: the fourth day.

God said, “Let the waters swarm with living creatures, and let birds fly over the earth, across the vault of the sky.” So God created the great sea creatures, and every kind of living thing that moves and swarms in the water, and every kind of winged bird. And God saw that it was good. God blessed them: “Be fruitful and multiply. Fill the waters of the seas — and let the birds multiply on the earth.” And there was evening, and there was morning: the fifth day.

God said, “Let the earth bring forth every kind of living creature: livestock, crawling things, and every kind of wild animal.” And so it was. God made every kind of wild animal, every kind of livestock, and everything that crawls on the ground. And God saw that it was good.

Then God said, “Let us make humanity in our image, after our likeness, and let them hold sway over the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, the livestock, the whole earth, and everything that crawls on it.” So God created humanity in his own image — in the image of God he created it; male and female he created them. God blessed them, and God said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply. Fill the earth and master it. Hold sway over the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, and every living thing that moves on the earth.” And God said, “Look — I have given you every seed-bearing plant on the face of the earth, and every tree with seed in its fruit. They are yours to eat. And to every wild animal, every bird of the sky, and everything that crawls on the earth with the breath of life in it, I give every green plant for food.” And so it was. And God saw all that he had made — and look, it was very good. And there was evening, and there was morning: the sixth day.

So the heavens and the earth were finished, and everything in them. On the seventh day God finished the work he had done, and on the seventh day he rested from all his work. God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it he rested from all the work of creating he had done.

This is the story of the heavens and the earth when they were created. On the day the LORD God made earth and heavens, no shrub of the field was yet on the earth and no plant of the field had sprouted — for the LORD God had not sent rain on the earth, and there was no human to work the soil — but a mist would rise from the earth and water the whole face of the ground. Then the LORD God formed the man from the dust of the ground, and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, and the man became a living being.

The LORD God planted a garden in Eden, in the east, and there he placed the man he had formed. And out of the ground the LORD God grew every tree that is pleasing to look at and good to eat from — with the tree of life in the middle of the garden, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

A river flows out of Eden to water the garden, and from there it divides into four branches. The first is named Pishon; it winds through the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold — and the gold of that land is good; bdellium is there, and lapis lazuli. The second river is named Gihon; it winds through the whole land of Cush. The third river is named Tigris; it runs east of Assyria. And the fourth river is the Euphrates.

The LORD God took the man and set him in the garden of Eden to work it and to watch over it. And the LORD God commanded the man: “You may eat freely from every tree in the garden — but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you may not eat. The day you eat from it, you die.”

Then the LORD God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a partner who matches him.” So the LORD God formed from the ground every wild animal and every bird of the sky, and brought them to the man to see what he would call them; and whatever the man called each living creature, that was its name. The man gave names to all the livestock, to the birds of the sky, and to every wild animal. But for the man himself, no matching partner was found.

So the LORD God put the man into a deep sleep, and while he slept, took one of his sides and closed up the flesh in its place. And the LORD God built the side he had taken from the man into a woman, and brought her to the man. And the man said: “This one, at last — bone of my bones, flesh of my flesh. This one will be called Woman, for from Man she was taken.” That is why a man leaves his father and mother and holds fast to his wife, and they become one flesh. And the two of them were naked, the man and his wife, and they felt no shame.

Now the serpent was the most cunning of all the wild animals the LORD God had made. He said to the woman, “Did God really say you can't eat from any tree in the garden?” The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat the fruit of the trees in the garden. It's only the fruit of the tree in the middle of the garden that God said, ‘Don't eat it — don't even touch it — or you will die.’” The serpent said to the woman, “You will not die. God knows that the day you eat from it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.” And the woman saw that the tree was good to eat from, and a delight to the eyes, and desirable for the wisdom it would give. She took its fruit and ate; and she gave some to her husband beside her, and he ate. Then the eyes of the two of them were opened, and they knew they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths.

They heard the sound of the LORD God walking in the garden in the evening breeze, and the man and his wife hid from the LORD God among the trees of the garden. The LORD God called to the man: “Where are you?” He said, “I heard the sound of you in the garden, and I was afraid because I was naked, so I hid.” And he said, “Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree I commanded you not to eat from?” The man said, “The woman you put beside me — she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate.” The LORD God said to the woman, “What have you done?” And the woman said, “The serpent tricked me, and I ate.”

So the LORD God said to the serpent: “Because you did this, you are cursed beyond all livestock and all wild animals. On your belly you will go, and dust you will eat, all the days of your life. I will set hatred between you and the woman, between your offspring and hers. He will strike your head, and you will strike his heel.”
To the woman he said: “I will make your pains in childbirth great; in pain you will bear children. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.”

And to the man he said: “Because you listened to your wife and ate from the tree I commanded you not to eat from, the ground is cursed because of you. In hard labor you will eat from it all the days of your life. Thorns and thistles it will grow for you, and you will eat the plants of the field. By the sweat of your face you will eat bread, until you return to the ground — for from it you were taken. You are dust, and to dust you will return.”
The man named his wife Eve, because she became the mother of all the living. And the LORD God made garments of skin for the man and his wife, and clothed them.

Then the LORD God said, “Look — the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. Now he must not be allowed to reach out his hand and take from the tree of life too, and eat, and live forever.” So the LORD God sent him out of the garden of Eden, to work the ground he had been taken from. He drove the man out; and east of the garden of Eden he stationed the cherubim, and a sword of flame turning every way, to guard the road to the tree of life.

The man knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and gave birth to Cain. She said, “I have made a man, with the LORD.” Then she gave birth to his brother Abel. Abel kept flocks; Cain worked the ground. In time Cain brought the LORD an offering from the fruit of the ground, and Abel brought some of the firstborn of his flock — the fat parts of them. The LORD looked on Abel and his offering, and on Cain and his offering he did not look. Cain was furious, and his face fell.

The LORD said to Cain, “Why are you furious? Why has your face fallen? If you do well, isn't there a lifting up? And if you don't do well, sin is crouching at the door — and its desire is for you, but you can master it.” And Cain said to his brother Abel — and while they were out in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him.

The LORD said to Cain, “Where is your brother Abel?” He said, “I don't know. Am I my brother's keeper?” And he said, “What have you done? Your brother's blood is crying out to me from the ground. And now you are cursed from the ground, which opened its mouth to take your brother's blood from your hand. When you work the ground, it will no longer give you its strength. You will be a restless wanderer on the earth.”

Cain said to the LORD, “My punishment is more than I can carry. Look — you have driven me today off the face of the ground, and I will be hidden from your face. I'll be a restless wanderer on the earth, and anyone who finds me will kill me.” The LORD said to him, “Then whoever kills Cain will be avenged seven times over.” And the LORD put a mark on Cain, so that no one who found him would strike him down. And Cain went out from the LORD's presence and settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden.

Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and gave birth to Enoch. And Cain was building a city, and he named the city after his son, Enoch. Irad was born to Enoch; Irad fathered Mehujael; Mehujael fathered Methushael; Methushael fathered Lamech. Lamech took two wives — one named Adah, the other Zillah. Adah gave birth to Jabal; he was the father of those who live in tents and keep livestock. His brother's name was Jubal; he was the father of all who play the lyre and the pipe. And Zillah gave birth to Tubal-cain, who forged every kind of tool of bronze and iron. Tubal-cain's sister was Naamah.

And Lamech said to his wives: “Adah and Zillah, hear my voice. Wives of Lamech, listen to what I say. I have killed a man for wounding me, a boy for striking me. If Cain is avenged seven times, then Lamech seventy-seven.”

The man knew his wife again, and she gave birth to a son and named him Seth — “because God has set in place another offspring for me instead of Abel, since Cain killed him.” And to Seth also a son was born, and he named him Enosh. That was when people began to call on the name of the LORD.

This is the book of the generations of Adam. On the day God created humankind, he made them in the likeness of God. Male and female he created them, and he blessed them and called their name Humankind on the day they were created. Adam lived a hundred and thirty years and fathered a son in his own likeness, after his image, and named him Seth. After Seth was born, Adam lived eight hundred years, and he fathered sons and daughters. All the days Adam lived were nine hundred and thirty years. And he died.

Seth lived a hundred and five years and fathered Enosh. After Enosh was born, Seth lived eight hundred and seven years, and he fathered sons and daughters. All the days of Seth were nine hundred and twelve years. And he died. Enosh lived ninety years and fathered Kenan. After Kenan was born, Enosh lived eight hundred and fifteen years, and he fathered sons and daughters. All the days of Enosh were nine hundred and five years. And he died. Kenan lived seventy years and fathered Mahalalel. After Mahalalel was born, Kenan lived eight hundred and forty years, and he fathered sons and daughters. All the days of Kenan were nine hundred and ten years. And he died.

Mahalalel lived sixty-five years and fathered Jared. After Jared was born, Mahalalel lived eight hundred and thirty years, and he fathered sons and daughters. All the days of Mahalalel were eight hundred and ninety-five years. And he died. Jared lived a hundred and sixty-two years and fathered Enoch. After Enoch was born, Jared lived eight hundred years, and he fathered sons and daughters. All the days of Jared were nine hundred and sixty-two years. And he died.

Enoch lived sixty-five years and fathered Methuselah. And Enoch walked with God three hundred years after Methuselah was born, and he fathered sons and daughters. All the days of Enoch were three hundred and sixty-five years. And Enoch walked with God — and he was not, because God took him.

Methuselah lived a hundred and eighty-seven years and fathered Lamech. After Lamech was born, Methuselah lived seven hundred and eighty-two years, and he fathered sons and daughters. All the days of Methuselah were nine hundred and sixty-nine years. And he died.

Lamech lived a hundred and eighty-two years and fathered a son. He named him Noah, saying, “This one will bring us relief from our work, from the painful labor of our hands, out of the ground the LORD has cursed.” After Noah was born, Lamech lived five hundred and ninety-five years, and he fathered sons and daughters. All the days of Lamech were seven hundred and seventy-seven years. And he died. And Noah was five hundred years old, and Noah fathered Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

When human beings began to multiply on the face of the ground and daughters were born to them, the sons of God saw that the daughters of human beings were beautiful, and they took as wives any they chose. And the LORD said, “My breath will not stay in a human being forever, because he is flesh. His days will be a hundred and twenty years.” The Nephilim were on the earth in those days — and afterward too — when the sons of God went in to the daughters of human beings and had children by them. Those were the mighty men of old, the men of renown.

And the LORD saw that human evil was great on the earth, and that every shape the thoughts of the heart took was nothing but evil, all day long. And the LORD was sorry that he had made human beings on the earth, and it grieved him to the heart. And the LORD said, “I will wipe the human beings I created off the face of the ground — human beings and animals and crawling things and birds of the sky. I am sorry that I made them.” But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.

These are the generations of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, blameless among the people of his time, and Noah walked with God. And Noah fathered three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. The earth was ruined in God's sight, and the earth was filled with violence. And God looked at the earth, and there it was, ruined — because all flesh had ruined its way on the earth.

And God said to Noah, “The end of all flesh has come before me. The earth is filled with violence because of them, and now I am going to ruin them, along with the earth. Make yourself an ark of cypress wood. Make rooms in the ark, and cover it inside and out with pitch. This is how you are to make it: the ark is to be three hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high. Make a roof for the ark and finish it to a cubit from the top. Put the door of the ark in its side, and make it with lower, second, and third decks.

“And look — I am bringing the flood of waters over the earth, to ruin all flesh with the breath of life in it under the sky. Everything on the earth will die. But I will establish my covenant with you, and you will come into the ark — you and your sons and your wife and your sons' wives with you. And from every living thing, from all flesh, bring two of every kind into the ark to keep them alive with you; they are to be male and female. From the birds after their kind, and the animals after their kind, and every crawling thing of the ground after its kind, two of every kind will come to you to be kept alive. And take with you every kind of food that is eaten, and store it up — it will be food for you and for them.” And Noah did it. Everything God commanded him, that is what he did.

And the LORD said to Noah, “Go into the ark, you and your whole household, because you are the one I have found righteous in front of me in this generation. Take with you seven pairs of every clean animal, male and female, and one pair of every animal that is not clean, male and female — and seven pairs of the birds of the sky as well, male and female, to keep offspring alive over the face of the whole earth. Because in seven days I will send rain on the earth for forty days and forty nights, and I will wipe every living thing I have made off the face of the ground.” And Noah did it. Everything the LORD commanded him, that is what he did.

Noah was six hundred years old when the flood of waters came over the earth. And Noah went into the ark, with his sons and his wife and his sons' wives, to get away from the waters of the flood. From the clean animals and the animals that are not clean, from the birds and everything that crawls on the ground, they came to Noah two by two into the ark, male and female, as God had commanded Noah. And after seven days the waters of the flood came over the earth.

In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month — on that very day all the springs of the great deep burst open, and the windows of the sky were opened. And the rain fell on the earth forty days and forty nights. On that same day Noah went into the ark, and Shem and Ham and Japheth, Noah's sons, and Noah's wife and the three wives of his sons with them — they, and every wild animal after its kind, and all the livestock after their kind, and every crawling thing that crawls on the earth after its kind, and every bird after its kind, every winged thing of every sort. They came to Noah into the ark, two by two, from all flesh with the breath of life in it. The ones that came in came in male and female, from all flesh, as God had commanded him. And the LORD shut him in.

And the flood came over the earth for forty days. The waters rose and lifted the ark, and it was raised high above the earth. The waters overpowered everything and rose greatly over the earth, and the ark drifted on the surface of the waters. The waters overpowered everything on the earth beyond measure, until all the high mountains under the whole sky were covered. Fifteen cubits above them the waters rose, and the mountains were covered.

And all flesh that moved on the earth died — birds, livestock, wild animals, every swarming thing that swarms on the earth, and every human being. Everything with the breath of life in its nostrils, everything on dry land, died. And he wiped out every living thing that was on the face of the ground — human beings and animals and crawling things and birds of the sky. They were wiped off the earth. Only Noah was left, and those with him in the ark. And the waters overpowered the earth for a hundred and fifty days.

And God remembered Noah, and all the wild animals and all the livestock with him in the ark. And God made a wind pass over the earth, and the waters went down. The springs of the deep and the windows of the sky were closed, and the rain from the sky was held back, and the waters drained off the earth steadily. At the end of a hundred and fifty days the waters had gone down, and in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat. The waters kept going down until the tenth month; in the tenth month, on the first day, the tops of the mountains appeared.

At the end of forty days Noah opened the window of the ark he had made, and he sent out a raven. It went back and forth until the waters had dried up from the earth. Then he sent out a dove, to see whether the waters had gone down from the face of the ground. But the dove found no place to set the sole of her foot, and she came back to him in the ark, because there was water over the face of the whole earth. He put out his hand and took her and brought her back inside with him. He waited another seven days and sent the dove out of the ark again. And the dove came back to him in the evening — and there in her beak was a freshly picked olive leaf. So Noah knew that the waters had gone down from the earth. He waited another seven days and sent out the dove, and she did not come back to him again.

In the six hundred and first year, in the first month, on the first day of the month, the waters had dried up from the earth. And Noah pulled back the covering of the ark and looked, and there it was: the face of the ground was dry. And in the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth was dry.

And God said to Noah, “Go out of the ark, you and your wife and your sons and your sons' wives with you. Bring out with you every living thing that is with you, from all flesh — birds and animals and every crawling thing that crawls on the earth — so they can swarm over the earth and be fruitful and multiply on it.” So Noah went out, and his sons and his wife and his sons' wives with him. Every wild animal, every crawling thing, every bird, everything that moves on the earth — they went out of the ark by families.

And Noah built an altar to the LORD, and he took some of every clean animal and every clean bird and offered burnt offerings on the altar. And the LORD smelled the soothing smell, and the LORD said in his heart, “I will never again curse the ground because of human beings, even though the shape of the human heart is evil from youth. And I will never again strike down every living thing, as I have done. As long as the earth lasts — seed time and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night will never stop.”

And God blessed Noah and his sons and said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth. The fear of you and the terror of you will be on every animal of the earth and every bird of the sky, on everything that crawls on the ground and all the fish of the sea. They are given into your hand. Every moving thing that is alive will be food for you; as I gave you the green plants, I now give you everything. But you must not eat flesh with its life in it — that is, its blood. And I will require a reckoning for your own lifeblood: from every animal I will require it, and from a human being. From a man for his brother I will require the life of a human being. Whoever sheds a human being's blood, by a human being his blood will be shed — because God made human beings in his own image. And you, be fruitful and multiply. Swarm over the earth and multiply on it.”

And God said to Noah and to his sons with him, “Look — I am establishing my covenant with you, and with your offspring after you, and with every living creature that is with you: the birds, the livestock, and every animal of the earth with you — everything that came out of the ark, every animal of the earth. I establish my covenant with you: never again will all flesh be cut off by the waters of a flood, and never again will there be a flood to ruin the earth.”

And God said, “This is the sign of the covenant I am making between me and you and every living creature that is with you, for all generations to come. I have set my bow in the cloud, and it will be the sign of the covenant between me and the earth. And when I bring clouds over the earth and the bow appears in the cloud, I will remember my covenant, which is between me and you and every living creature, all flesh — and the waters will never again become a flood to ruin all flesh. The bow will be in the cloud, and I will look at it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature, all flesh that is on the earth.” And God said to Noah, “This is the sign of the covenant I have established between me and all flesh that is on the earth.”
The sons of Noah who came out of the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Ham was the father of Canaan. These three were Noah's sons, and from them the whole earth was populated.

And Noah, a man of the soil, was the first to plant a vineyard. He drank some of the wine and got drunk, and he lay uncovered inside his tent. And Ham, the father of Canaan, saw his father's nakedness, and he told his two brothers outside. So Shem and Japheth took a cloak, laid it across both their shoulders, and walked in backward, and covered their father's nakedness. Their faces were turned away, and they did not see their father's nakedness.

When Noah woke up from his wine and learned what his youngest son had done to him, he said: “Cursed be Canaan. The lowest of slaves he will be to his brothers.” And he said: “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem; and let Canaan be his slave. May God make room for Japheth, and let him live in the tents of Shem; and let Canaan be his slave.” And Noah lived three hundred and fifty years after the flood. All the days of Noah were nine hundred and fifty years. And he died.
